questions.q: Doping silicon with a pentavalent impurity such as phosphorus produces:
questions.solution:
Phosphorus has **five** valence electrons. Four form covalent bonds with neighbouring silicon atoms, leaving the fifth loosely bound and easily freed.

So the majority carriers are **electrons** and the material is **n-type**. The dopant is called a **donor**.

A **trivalent** dopant such as boron leaves a vacancy — a **hole** — giving p-type material, and is called an **acceptor**.

In both cases the crystal remains **electrically neutral overall**; doping changes which carriers are plentiful, not the net charge.

questions.q: In a forward-biased p-n junction, the width of the depletion region:
questions.solution:
Forward bias applies the positive terminal to the p-side, which **opposes** the built-in potential barrier and pushes majority carriers towards the junction.

The depletion region therefore **narrows** and the barrier height falls, so a large current flows.

Reverse bias does the opposite: the depletion region **widens**, the barrier rises, and only a tiny leakage current due to minority carriers flows.

questions.q: The ripple frequency at the output of a full-wave rectifier fed from a $50\ \text{Hz}$ supply is:
questions.solution:
A **full-wave** rectifier uses **both** halves of each input cycle, inverting the negative half rather than discarding it. So there are **two** output pulses per input cycle:

$f_{\text{ripple}} = 2 \times 50 = \mathbf{100\ \text{Hz}}$

A **half-wave** rectifier discards one half-cycle, so its ripple is $50\ \text{Hz}$.

The higher ripple frequency is an advantage: it is easier to smooth with a given filter capacitor, which is one reason full-wave rectification is preferred.

questions.q: The Zener diode is primarily used as :
questions.solution: In reverse breakdown the voltage across a Zener diode stays almost constant over a wide range of current, so it holds a load's voltage steady: a **voltage regulator**.

questions.q: For a transistor to work as an amplifier, the emitter-base junction and the collector-base junction must be:
questions.solution:
Active-region operation requires the **emitter-base junction forward biased** and the **collector-base junction reverse biased**.

Forward bias on the emitter junction injects carriers into the thin, lightly doped base; reverse bias on the collector junction sweeps them across. The base is deliberately **thin and lightly doped** so that most carriers pass through rather than recombining.

Both junctions forward biased gives **saturation**, both reverse gives **cut-off** — the two states used for switching rather than amplification.

questions.q: Which gate is called a universal gate?
questions.solution:
**NAND** is universal, and so is NOR: any logic function whatever can be built from NAND gates alone.

A NAND with both inputs tied together gives NOT; NAND followed by NOT gives AND; and inverting both inputs of a NAND gives OR by De Morgan's theorem.

This matters industrially — a manufacturer can fabricate one gate type and build everything from it, which is simpler and cheaper than making several.

questions.q: To obtain sustained oscillation in an oscillator,
questions.solution: These are the Barkhausen conditions: the loop gain $A\beta$ must be 1, and the total phase shift round the loop must be $0$ or $2\pi$, which is **positive** feedback. **All the above**.

questions.q: The value of forbidden energy gap for Si at room temperature is :
questions.solution:
Silicon's band gap is about **1.1 eV**. An energy gap is measured in electronvolts, not volts, which rules out two options at once.

0.7 V is the barrier potential of a silicon p-n junction, a different quantity. (The 2023 paper asked this too.)

questions.q: The output of a two-input AND gate is HIGH when:
questions.solution:
An **AND** gate outputs 1 only when **both** inputs are 1 — it implements multiplication, $Y = A \cdot B$.

For comparison: **OR** is HIGH when at least one input is HIGH; **XOR** when exactly one is; **NAND** is the inverse of AND, so it is LOW only when both inputs are HIGH.

questions.q: A transistor has $\alpha = 0.98$. Find its current gain $\beta$ in common-emitter configuration.
questions.solution:
$\beta = \dfrac{\alpha}{1 - \alpha} = \dfrac{0.98}{1 - 0.98} = \dfrac{0.98}{0.02} = \mathbf{49}$

Note how sensitive $\beta$ is to $\alpha$: raising $\alpha$ from $0.98$ to $0.99$ would take $\beta$ from 49 to 99. This is why the base must be made very thin — a small improvement in the fraction of carriers reaching the collector doubles the gain.

questions.q: A transistor has $\beta = 100$ and a base current of $20\ \mu\text{A}$. Find the collector current, in milliamperes.
questions.solution:
$I_C = \beta I_B = 100 \times 20\times10^{-6} = 2\times10^{-3}\ \text{A} = \mathbf{2\ \text{mA}}$

The emitter current is then $I_E = I_B + I_C = 2.02\ \text{mA}$.

questions.q: Determine the wavelength of the light emitted from LED, which is made up of GaAsP semiconductor, whose forbidden energy gap is 1.875 eV. Give the wavelength in nanometres. (Given $h = 6.6\times10^{-34}$ Js)
questions.solution:
$\lambda = \dfrac{hc}{E_g} = \dfrac{6.6\times10^{-34} \times 3\times10^{8}}{1.875 \times 1.6\times10^{-19}} = \dfrac{1.98\times10^{-25}}{3.0\times10^{-19}} = 6.6\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$

$\lambda = \mathbf{660\ nm}$, which is **red** light — the colour the paper also asks for.

questions.q: A half-wave rectifier is fed from a $50\ \text{Hz}$ supply. Find the ripple frequency of its output, in hertz.
questions.solution:
A half-wave rectifier passes only one half of each cycle, giving **one** pulse per input cycle.

Ripple frequency $= \mathbf{50\ \text{Hz}}$, the same as the supply. A full-wave rectifier would give $100\ \text{Hz}$.

questions.q: How many rows are there in the truth table of a three-input logic gate?
questions.solution:
Each input is either 0 or 1, so with $n$ inputs there are $2^{n}$ combinations.

$2^{3} = \mathbf{8}$ rows.

questions.q: Explain the construction and working of an n-p-n transistor as a common-emitter amplifier. Derive the relations between the currents and between $\alpha$ and $\beta$, and explain why the base is made thin and lightly doped.
questions.solution:
**Construction.** An n-p-n transistor is a thin layer of p-type semiconductor — the **base** — sandwiched between two n-type regions, the **emitter** and the **collector**.

The three regions are deliberately **not** symmetrical:

**Emitter** — heavily doped, moderate size. Its job is to supply carriers in quantity.

**Base** — very thin (of order $10^{-6}\ \text{m}$) and **lightly** doped.

**Collector** — moderately doped and **physically largest**, because it must dissipate the heat.

**Biasing.** For amplification the transistor is operated in the **active region**: the **emitter-base junction is forward biased** and the **collector-base junction reverse biased**.

**Working.** Forward bias on the emitter junction injects a large number of **electrons** from the emitter into the base.

In the base these electrons are minority carriers among the holes. A few recombine, giving a small **base current** $I_B$. But because the base is thin and lightly doped, **the great majority — about $95$ to $99\%$ — diffuse straight across** into the collector junction, where the reverse-bias field sweeps them into the collector.

The result is a large **collector current** $I_C$ controlled by a small $I_B$.

**As an amplifier.** The input signal is applied between base and emitter, in series with the forward bias; the output is taken across a load resistance $R_L$ in the collector circuit.

A small change in $V_{BE}$ produces a small change in $I_B$, which produces a **much larger** change in $I_C$, and hence a large change in the voltage across $R_L$. The voltage gain is

$A_V = \beta \times \dfrac{R_L}{r_i}$

The common-emitter amplifier also introduces a **$180^\circ$ phase shift**: as $I_C$ rises, the drop across $R_L$ rises, so the collector voltage **falls**.

**The current relations.** By Kirchhoff's junction rule applied to the transistor as a node:

$\boxed{I_E = I_B + I_C}$

The two current gains are defined as

$\alpha = \dfrac{I_C}{I_E}$ (common base) and $\beta = \dfrac{I_C}{I_B}$ (common emitter)

**Deriving the relation between them.** Start from $I_E = I_B + I_C$ and divide throughout by $I_C$:

$\dfrac{I_E}{I_C} = \dfrac{I_B}{I_C} + 1$

$\dfrac{1}{\alpha} = \dfrac{1}{\beta} + 1 = \dfrac{1 + \beta}{\beta}$

$\boxed{\alpha = \dfrac{\beta}{1 + \beta}}$ and inverting, $\boxed{\beta = \dfrac{\alpha}{1 - \alpha}}$

**Why the base is thin and lightly doped.** This is the heart of the design, and both properties serve the same end: **minimising recombination in the base**.

**Thin**, so that an injected electron has only a very short distance to cross and little time in which to meet a hole.

**Lightly doped**, so that there are few holes there to meet in the first place.

Together these ensure that nearly every carrier leaving the emitter reaches the collector, making $\alpha$ close to 1.

**And $\beta$ is extraordinarily sensitive to exactly that.** Since $\beta = \dfrac{\alpha}{1 - \alpha}$, the denominator is a small difference between two nearly equal numbers:

$\alpha = 0.95 \Rightarrow \beta = 19$

$\alpha = 0.98 \Rightarrow \beta = 49$

$\alpha = 0.99 \Rightarrow \beta = 99$

$\alpha = 0.995 \Rightarrow \beta = 199$

A change in $\alpha$ of less than a percent **doubles** the gain. So the thin lightly doped base is not a refinement — it is the single design feature that decides whether the device amplifies usefully at all, and it is why transistor manufacture demands such precise control of layer thickness.

**Why the emitter is heavily doped** follows from the same reasoning: a large injected current gives a large $I_C$, and heavy doping ensures the current across the emitter junction consists almost entirely of electrons flowing **into** the base rather than holes flowing back out of it.
